findings.title: Denial cache key omits identity type, allowing cross-identity collisions
findings.body: The new denial cache key is built from `checkReq.Namespace.Value`, `checkReq.UserUID`, action, name and parent folder, but not from `checkReq.IdentityType`. `validateSubject` returns only the raw id portion of the subject, so different identity types can produce the same `UserUID` — e.g. `anonymous:0` and `render:0` both yield `"0"` (both forms are exercised in the tests). A denial recorded for one identity type therefore short-circuits checks for the other identity type within the same namespace, which can deny an access that should be allowed (for instance the render service, whose permissions are synthesized separately in `getRendererPermissions`, for up to the 30s TTL). Note also that the permission cache deliberately uses a distinct key per identity type (`anonymousPermCacheKey` vs `userPermCacheKey`), so the denial cache is inconsistent with it.

findings.title: Ambiguous denial cache key from unescaped concatenation of name and parent
findings.body: `userPermDenialCacheKey` concatenates action, resource name and parent folder with `"_"` separators. Since Grafana UIDs may contain underscores, distinct requests map to the same key: e.g. name="a_b", parent="c" and name="a", parent="b_c" both produce `<ns>.perm_<uid>_<action>_a_b_c`. A cached denial for one resource then wrongly denies a different resource the user may actually be allowed to access, for the lifetime of the entry (30s). Using a separator that cannot appear in UIDs, or hashing/length-prefixing the components, would avoid this.

findings.title: Every non-allowed Check now issues DB queries even with a warm permission cache
findings.body: The cache lookup was removed from `getUserPermissions`/`getAnonymousPermissions`, and `Check` only returns early when the cached permissions grant access. Any check that is not granted by the cached scope map falls through to `getIdentityPermissions`, which re-reads basic roles, teams and permissions from the database (`permissionStore.GetUserPermissions`) even though a fresh cache entry exists. Workloads that check many resources a user cannot see (list/search filtering, authorization probes on many dashboard UIDs) will now generate one full permission query per distinct (name, folder) pair until the denial cache entry is written, which can be a large multiplier on DB load compared to the previous behaviour where the cache served all of them. Consider only re-querying when the cache entry is older than some threshold, or dedup/throttle the refresh.

findings.title: Cached denial short-circuits the DB re-query, so newly granted permissions are invisible for up to 30s
findings.body: `Check` returns immediately on a denial cache hit (line 117) before the permission cache / DB fallback runs, and a denial is cached for every negative result (line 154, shortCacheTTL = 30s). This re-introduces exactly the staleness the PR aims to fix for the case where a Check on a given (name, folder) pair happens before the permission is granted — e.g. a probe for a dashboard/folder UID that is created immediately afterwards, or a permission grant on an existing resource. The subsequent DB re-query cannot correct the result because the denial entry wins. Also, for inherited access the fallback re-reads permissions but still uses the cached `folderTree` (`buildFolderTree`, 30s TTL), so a dashboard placed in a brand-new sub-folder is denied and that denial is then cached, even though fresh folder data would allow it. At minimum the denial cache should be bypassed/invalidated when the underlying folder tree or permissions are refreshed.

findings.title: permissionCacheUsage metric no longer reflects cache hits in Check
findings.body: In `Check`, `permissionCacheUsage` is incremented with `"true"` only when the cached permissions actually allow the request, and the unconditional `"false"` increment at line 137 is reached on every cache hit that did not grant access. The metric therefore measures "allowed from cache" rather than cache hit ratio, and cache hits that end in a denial are reported as misses. Dashboards/alerts built on this metric will show a large, misleading drop in cache hit rate after this change.

findings.title: Denial-cache test does not actually verify the short-circuit
findings.body: In "Should deny on explicit cache deny entry" the permission cache is seeded with `map[string]bool{"dashboards:uid:dash1": false}` under a comment claiming it "allow[s] access to the dashboard to prove this is not checked". A `false` value means not allowed, so `checkPermission` returns false, the code falls through to the DB (empty `fakeStore`, no permissions) and still denies. The assertion `assert.False(resp.Allowed)` passes whether or not the denial cache is consulted, so the new short-circuit path is untested. The value should be `true` (and ideally the fake store should also grant the permission) so that a regression removing the denial-cache lookup makes the test fail.
